say: Welcome. This is one story across two apps. We compare three short files, build and check a project brief in Word, then turn it into a six-slide deck in PowerPoint.
Success today is a workable draft, not a polished publication. We have about sixty minutes. The suggested minutes sit in the corner and you start the timer yourself.
One rule runs through everything: review before using. Proposed is not approved.
welcome.ask: What usually goes wrong when a draft mixes what people asked for with what has been approved?
welcome.watch: Say the rule out loud now. Learners who skip it tend to let a proposal slip into the brief as a fact.

say: Three files, three roles. The community summary says what people reported. The inspection register says what was seen and what is only proposed. The PDF holds risks, dependencies and indicative priorities.
The four labels on this page are the vocabulary for the whole session. Each one has a word and a shape, so nobody relies on colour alone.
The source rule: the three files hold the facts. The website image, which we capture later, is only for the look.
sources.ask: Which of the three files could you least trust to show that work is approved?
sources.watch: Learners often treat the PDF as the final word. Point out that it also says it records no approved decisions.

say: Download the ZIP. It holds the three files. You can also download each file on its own.
Save them where Word can reach them, for example OneDrive. Copilot in Word needs to be able to see the files.
Everything here is fictional training material.
get.ask: Where did you save the files, and can Word open that location?
get.watch: A file saved only on the desktop is the usual reason Copilot cannot find it later.

say: Four things should be true before we start: files saved, Word and PowerPoint ready with Copilot, two windows you can switch between, and a page that remembers your step.
Do not use real or personal documents. The three practice files give everyone the same context.
needs.ask: Can you switch between this page and Word without losing your place?
needs.watch: If a learner's Word has no Copilot button, sort that out now rather than in the middle of Prompt 1.

say: Open Word, start a new working document and open Copilot. Add or reference the three files, then copy and run Prompt 1.
The prompt asks for four headings: Confirmed, Proposed, Conflicting and Needs validation. It also asks for the supporting file for each finding.
While it works, think about where each finding belongs. Return here when the four categories appear.
w1.ask: Which finding do you expect to land under Conflicting?
w1.watch: Hover over the Copy button to show the prompt anatomy. The last sentence is the guard: community requests are not approved decisions.

say: Use the real answer in Copilot, not the picture. Tick what you can see. Nothing is scored.
The two checks that matter most: every finding names its supporting file, and conflicts are visible rather than smoothed over.
w1c.ask: Did Copilot treat any community request as an approved need?
w1c.watch: Typical gaps: a missing source file for a finding, or a proposal sitting under Confirmed.

say: Prompt 2 asks for a concise project brief with nine sections. The list is on the page, so learners can check the structure as it appears.
Anything proposed, indicative or unresolved should carry a visible label. That is the thing to watch while Copilot drafts.
Return after the draft is generated.
w2.ask: Is the section structure suitable for a stakeholder who has not seen the files?
w2.watch: If generation is slow, use the time to talk through the checklist. Do not add another activity.

say: Check the draft against five points. The brief uses only the three files. The summary leads with findings, risks and decisions. Confirmed and proposed are not blended.
No owner, approval, date or commitment may be invented. And the brief should be short enough to become a presentation.
w2c.ask: Did you find any owner, date or approval that is not in the files?
w2c.watch: Invented owners are the most common fault. Ask learners to find the sentence in a source file that supports each one.

say: Checkpoint one. Compare and draft are done. Next is one improvement to the brief.
If proposed items are not labelled in your draft, go back to the draft step before moving on.
cp1.ask: Is anything in your brief shown as decided that is only proposed?
cp1.watch: Use the Flow overview button to show the eight stages and jump between them.

say: Choose one option and run only that prompt. Option A turns the proposed improvements into a table. Option B rewrites the executive summary so findings, risks and decisions come first.
Improve one section, not the whole document. Do not run both.
w3.ask: Which section would help your readers most if it were easier to scan?
w3.watch: This step is optional. If time is short, skip it. The flow is not blocked and nothing later depends on it.

say: Three checks. The section is easier to scan. All qualifications are still there. And you improved only one section.
If you skipped this step, nothing is missing. Carry on to validation.
w3c.ask: Did the table or the new summary keep every Proposed and Indicative label?
w3c.watch: A tidy table that drops the word proposed is worse than the untidy original.

say: Prompt 4 checks your brief against the three files. It flags unsupported statements, inconsistencies, missing qualifications and any proposal or indicative date shown as confirmed.
Apply the corrections before you move to PowerPoint. Save the brief as Community Facilities Improvement Program, dash, Project Brief.
You need a sound working brief, not a fully polished publication.
w4.ask: What did Copilot flag that you had not noticed?
w4.watch: Learners may accept every suggestion. Remind them to check each correction against the source, because validation can also introduce errors.

say: Five checks. Every material statement traces to a source. Unsupported claims are removed or qualified. Proposed work stays proposed, and indicative dates and priorities stay indicative.
The last one is the important one: you applied the corrections before moving on.
w4c.ask: Is the brief saved under the required name?
w4c.watch: PowerPoint will use this file as its main source, so an unsaved or renamed copy causes trouble in the next step.

say: Checkpoint two. The Word part is done. Three inputs feed the deck, and each has a role.
The Word brief is the narrative and the source of slide messages. The PDF supports with risks, dependencies and detail. The website image is a visual reference only.
Content boundary: the image guides design only. Project facts come from the validated brief and the PDF.
trans.ask: Why must the website text never end up on a slide?
trans.watch: Say it plainly. Some learners expect Copilot to pull content from the image.

say: Open the reference website in your browser and capture the entire page. Save the image with a clear filename, then come back.
If the capture is slow or fails, choose Use backup capture. It downloads a ready image. That is not a failure. The goal is to use a visual reference, not to master screenshot software.
cap.ask: Does your capture show enough of the page to show the overall look?
cap.watch: Do not let anyone spend more than a few minutes here. Push people to the backup early.

say: Three checks. The capture shows enough of the page to show the visual system. It is readable as a PowerPoint reference. And you understand the website text is not project evidence.
capc.ask: Is the image ready to add to PowerPoint?
capc.watch: A tiny or cropped capture gives Copilot very little to follow. The backup image is a fair swap.

say: In PowerPoint, open Copilot and create a presentation from the brief, the PDF and the capture image. Run Prompt 5.
The prompt separates three roles: the brief for the narrative, the PDF for evidence, the image for the look. The six slides are on the page.
The first deck is a draft. Copilot may follow the image only loosely. It is a guide, not a template. Return when six slides are present.
p5.ask: Which slide do you expect to be the hardest to get right?
p5.watch: While it generates, walk through the review checklist on the next page. Do not start another task.

say: Six checks. Six slides. The brief provides the narrative. The PDF strengthens evidence without replacing it. The image affects design only. Slide text is shorter than the Word document. Proposals and unresolved matters are labelled.
p5c.ask: Is any slide a copy-paste of a Word section?
p5c.watch: Dense slides are the usual problem. That is a good lead-in to the next step.

say: Improve one slide only: Risks and decisions required. Prompt 6 asks Copilot to separate confirmed risks, unresolved questions and decisions required, using only the brief and the PDF.
Keep the deck's existing look. This is a single, small improvement, not a redesign.
p6.ask: Can your audience tell a confirmed risk from an open question at a glance?
p6.watch: This step is optional. If time is short, skip it. The flow is not blocked.

say: Five checks. One clear message. The three groups are distinct. No unsupported claim has crept in. The hierarchy matches the rest of the deck, and it reads well in presentation mode.
p6c.ask: Did the improved slide add any fact that is not in the brief or the PDF?
p6c.watch: Look for invented owners or dates in the decisions column.

say: One combined review of both files. The brief uses only the three files. Confirmed and proposed are not blended. No owner, approval, date or commitment is invented.
The deck has six slides. The PDF supports evidence only. The website image affects design only. Proposals and unresolved matters are labelled, and slide text is shorter than the Word document.
Save both files under the names shown before you finish.
final.ask: Which check was the hardest to pass?
final.watch: Ticks are for self-review. Nothing is scored and nothing locks Next.

say: Evidence, then a Word brief, then a design reference, then a stakeholder deck.
Word develops and validates the narrative. PowerPoint communicates that narrative visually. The PDF supports the evidence, while the website capture guides the design.
recap.ask: Where in that flow would a wrong fact do the most damage?
recap.watch: Keep the close short. Three minutes.

say: Five skills: compare evidence, draft a grounded brief, improve one section, validate against the sources, and turn it into six slides.
Three habits: review before using, remember that proposed is not approved, and keep the source roles apart.
Which prompt will you reuse this week?
learned.ask: Which prompt will you reuse this week?
learned.watch: Ask for one concrete use at work, not a general intention.
